place.en: The hidden realm · The stone chamber

setup.zh: 墙后面是一间石室，四个空坑，一边七拃；石台上一只玉匣，匣子里一撮土。银月嫌这屋里的气冲得像陈年老酒，丢下一句「本王睡一觉」，钻回了木牌。墙缝里站着一个黄袍，笑眯眯的：「会自己长的土？」
setup.en: Behind the wall, a stone chamber: four empty pits, seven hand-spans a side; on the altar a jade box, and in the box a pinch of earth. Yinyue declares the air in here as strong as old wine, says "This king is taking a nap," and slips back into the token. In the crack of the wall stands a yellow robe, smiling: "Earth that grows by itself?"

recap.zh: 石室里一撮息壤。赤松观的邹青松追了你一路：火蛇、那面「结丹以下，无人能破」的盾；干河床的黑里，阿禾两句话、一根藤，四个贪心的人替你挨了他的火；踏马的符一跳，你落在蛫背后，火蛇撞灭在龟壳上。银月两根狐毛破了他的盾，你自己结果了他。你坐进息壤，它长进你身子里，五门俱开，练气四层。
recap.en: A pinch of xirang in the stone chamber. Zou Qingsong of the Red Pine Abbey chased you the length of the realm: fire snakes, and a shield nothing short of Core Formation can break. In the dark of the dry riverbed, two lines and one vine from A He set four greedy men on him in your place. One leap on the Hoof-It Charm put you behind the gui, and the fire snakes died on its shell. Yinyue broke his shield with two hairs from her tail; you finished him yourself. You sat in the xirang and it grew into you: all five doors open, layer four of Qi Refining.

zh: 一张石台，一只玉匣。「息壤。」
四面火蛇。腰带夹层里那匹歪马，往脚底一拍。
en: A stone altar, a jade box. "Xirang."
Fire snakes on four sides. The crooked horse from his belt fold, slapped on his sole.

story.zh:
墙后面，是一间石室，方方正正，四壁青石打磨得光溜溜的，照得出人影。没有灵草，没有法器，也没有前人的骸骨，干干净净，像是昨天才有人扫过。西北角贴着地，有一个半人高的黑洞，墙外那股风，便是一阵一阵往那洞里吸的。正中一张石台，台上一只玉匣。可小满一进门，最先看见的，却不是那只玉匣。石室的地上，离石台三步远的地方，有四个坑。

四个方方的坑，一边一个，排成一个四方，每个有碗口大，一尺来深，坑底磨得溜光，坑沿磨得发亮，一圈青苔，青得发黑，青苔底下透着一点幽幽的绿光，凑近了，一股凉凉的铜腥气。他爹教过他看蹄印：印子深，是那东西沉；印子磨得发亮，是那东西在这里站了很久很久。一样极沉极沉的东西，四条腿，把石头都站出了坑。然后，它走了。

小满蹲下来，张开手掌，拇指抵着一个坑的外沿，一拃一拃地量到另一个坑的外沿——猎户量蹄印，向来是这么量的。一拃，两拃，三拃……七拃。另外三边，边边都是七拃。他想起二试那个老执事讲的：一千个人下泗水捞鼎，没捞着。这间石室里的灵气厚得化不开，外头的却薄得像刷锅水；他站在四个空坑中间，头一回隐隐约约地觉得，这两件事，也许是一件事。

石室的四壁，走近了才看得出有刻痕，极浅，极细。东墙是水，浪头卷着浪头，水里漂着房子，漂着伸着手的人。南墙是一个人，背着一只筐，从筐里抓出什么往水里撒，撒过的地方，水底下冒出一块一块的地来；那人的腰是弯的，像背着一样极重极重的东西。西墙是九样东西，三排，一排三个，每一样都四四方方，底下四只脚，两只耳朵。北墙是空的，刻满了浅浅的格子，格子里什么都没有；最底下，贴着地，有一个很小的刻痕，刻得比别的都深，都新：一只狐狸，蜷着身子，尾巴绕着身子，跟他胸口那块木牌上的，一模一样。银月跳下他的肩膀，走到那只刻出来的狐狸跟前，低下头，拿鼻子碰了碰它，尾巴垂着，又跳回他肩上，一句话也没有说。

他走到石台前，打开了玉匣。匣盖一掀，满屋子的灵气往匣口轻轻一沉，像一屋子的水找着了低处。匣子里，只有**一撮土**。黄褐色的，松松的，刚好铺满匣底，跟他家后院那块种不出东西的地里的土没什么两样。小满盯着看了半天，道：「……就这？」肩上的银月却一字一字地道：「[息壤]{注=xirang}。」她的声音在抖，尾巴尖上的毛一根一根全竖了起来，「会自己长的土。你给它一粒，它长出一撮；给它一撮，它长出一座山。当年——」她停住了，像在很深的井里捞一样东西，捞了半天，只捞上来半桶。她盯着地上那四个空坑，没有再往下说。小满等了一会儿，问：「那面墙后头有风——你早知道，里头是它？」她隔了一会儿，才回过头来，一双金色的眼睛亮得有些发潮：「……本王只闻得出墙后头有一样会长的东西。是什么，本王想不起来。本王只知道，你是漏勺。」她把头转回去，声音低得像自言自语：「一个漏勺，夜夜在柴垛上坐到后半夜，漏一夜，接着坐。坐了一年。……本王看着烦。」小满想说句什么，想起的又是那个「谢」字——在蒙山的柴垛上欠下的，欠到今天，还没还上。

她的鼻子又抽了两抽，打了个喷嚏。她一张嘴，屋里的气便往她嘴里灌。「这屋里的气，冲得像一坛子陈年老酒。」她道，「本王睡一觉。谁也别吵。」话音一落，她化作一缕银光，钻回了木牌。木牌凉了，凉得像井底的一块石头。

他合上玉匣，盘腿坐在石台跟前等她醒，等了一顿饭的工夫，又一顿饭的工夫。她没说这土拿来做什么，他便不动它。石室里静得听得见西北角那个黑洞里的风，一吸，一停。

话分两头。那一日小满钻进凶崖，阿禾跟着人多的走——长廊通园子，她要那株紫须芝——可人多的地方，落下来的刀也多。

进门以前，她看见了两样东西：卖地图那两个里头抄着手的那一个，人人往门里挤，他不挤，眼睛钉在沈小满身上；老蔫肩上，斜挎着一大盘麻绳。进秘境捡灵草，用不着那么长的绳子。她在本子上记了一笔：**马小宝，麻绳一盘。——凶崖？**没有回头。

她照着肚子里那张图走。第二间石室门口，地上第三块石板踩上去会翻——她站在旁边，喊了一声「别踩第三块」。一个听了；一个没来得及听，给后头一个锦袍公子一肘子拐开，掉了下去，坑里「哎哟」一声，是孙二狗的嗓子。她给人群推着往前走，回头喊了第二声，没有人应。

石桥窄，只容一个人。她走到桥头，桥当中黑地里撞上了两个人，一个本观的灰袍，一个青萍的青袍，隔着三步站住了，谁也看不清谁的脸。站了很久，两个人都不动，都不让。灰袍伸手往怀里一摸——青袍的剑先出了鞘。灰袍倒下去，手里攥着的，是一只火折子。青袍跨过他，过了桥。阿禾在桥头的石头后头蹲了一炷香，才敢过去。

桥那头的灵草园子，最后一株给人连根拔了。两个本观的老弟子把一个锦袍公子按进泥里，按到他不动了，才松手，蹲在泥里分那株草，一人一半；又翻他的荷包，灵石五块，一人两块，多出来那一块，两个人猜拳。园子底下那道干河床，地图上画的是水；今年水退得低，露了底，石缝里一丛一丛全是灵草，上中下三品都有，壁上一道铜矿。人都往下涌。往下只有一道石坎，一人宽。坎口站着内门的祁长松，八层，袍子下摆一层土黄的灰，两只脚钉在那里；人涌到他跟前，推他，挤他，像水撞上一根桩，撞不动，只好从两边分开，又流回来。坎底下，那四个九层一丛一丛地拔，拔一丛，往袖里一揣，看都不看是几品。拔够了上来，祁长松才挪开一步。

阿禾没有去抢。她四层，功法是养草木的，打架是她最不会的一样；坎底下那四个九层，坎口那一个八层，哪一个都是一袖子拂她两三丈的人。她绕着河床边上，往没人的那一头走，走到尽头，有一片地，是黑的，黑得发亮，一根草也不长，跟石坳村她家那面坡田，一个样子。黑地的边上，偏偏冒着一株草，三片叶子，紫里透金，叶背上一层细绒，在黑地里自己透着一点暗金的光，像三盏熬到了底的小油灯：「紫须芝，一株抵三块灵石。」三块灵石，是外门一个月的份例。她蹲下去，指头底下的黑土一松，露出半粒东西来，黑的，硬得像石子：是谷，烧焦了一样的谷。她拿指甲再往下抠——那片黑地底下，一垄一垄，排得整整齐齐。很久以前，这里有人种过地。那株紫须芝的根，正缠在那一垄谷里：拔草，便连根带谷翻成一团烂泥。她没有拔。她从那一垄的这一头，离草根远远的，一粒一粒，抠出三粒来，草根一根也没伤着。

抠出第三粒，她眼角里一亮。

不是火光，是气。观天之道，头一样学的就是看气：这片黑地里，草木的气是一缕一缕的青烟，那株紫须芝顶上的一缕最亮，像一根灯芯；地底下那一垄死谷，冷冰冰的，一丝也没有。可园子那头，有一团气正顺着河床边上过来——人身上的气厚厚一层，沉得压人，隔着半片园子，压得她胸口一紧；手里还托着一团火，红得发紫，比人更旺。那团火走到哪里，两边草木的青烟便往回一缩，缩成一线，像给人掐住了脖子。

阿禾的手停在了土里。

河滩上那个托赤铜葫芦的黄袍。九层，远在她之上；何况她的功法是养草木的，攻不了人，正面撞上，是一个死。那团火又近了十步。她低头一看，自己指缝里也冒着一缕青——她的气，在这片光秃秃的黑地上，亮得像一盏灯。

她把三粒谷攥进手心，另一只手往袖子里一摸，摸出一张符来——师父压在她袖子里、说「不到要命的时候别动」的三张符，这是头一张：隐身符。符往心口一贴，一凉，她低头一看，自己的手没了，指缝里那缕青也没了，连脚底下的影子也没了。黑地边上裂着一道石缝，一尺来宽，她侧身滑了进去，脸贴着凉土，一动不动，一口气喘得比草叶还轻。

来的果然是他，白净脸，赭黄袍子，笑眯眯的。黑地边上那三盏小油灯，他一眼就看见了。看见的不止他一个：园子里猜拳赢了那一块灵石的老弟子，也从另一头扑了过来，手先伸到了草上。黄袍没有出声，右手大拇指一顶，铜塞子拔了出来，一条火蛇从葫芦嘴里窜出去，在那人脖子上绕了一圈。那人只叫了半声。火蛇缩回来，他低头看了一眼葫芦嘴，才把塞子塞了回去。阿禾在石缝里，一样一样看着：他身上那口气厚得很，可杀人，他一丝也不动自己的，全使葫芦里的火；盾挎在左臂，葫芦托在右手；动一回手，是拔一下塞子，再塞一下塞子——拔塞子、塞塞子那一下，他的眼睛要离开人，看一眼葫芦嘴。那一下，是他最慢的时候。

他弯腰把那株紫须芝连根拔了，那一垄谷翻成了一团烂泥。他又蹲下去翻那人的怀，摸出三块灵石，连草一起揣进怀里——离她那道石缝，不到三步，她看得见他靴子帮上的泥。他站起来，往四下里看了一眼，神识也跟着贴地扫了一圈——阿禾脊梁上一凉，像有一根冰凉的手指头划过去。师父说过，这张符，九层以下的眼睛看不穿，神识也扫不穿；那一凉滑过石缝，没有停。坎底下九层在拔，坎口八层在守，这一片园子，拔秃了。他像想起了一件什么事，笑了一笑，自言自语道：「门口那盘麻绳……」

那盘麻绳，他在河滩上便瞧见了：沉鼎观一个胖墩墩的少爷，身后跟班肩上斜挎着一大盘。进秘境捡灵草，用不着那么长的绳子。凶崖，图上只有一行字——没人去。没人去的地方，才有东西；一盘绳子往没人去的地方走，是去捆东西的。他把葫芦往腰上一掖，往石厅那头去了，走得很快。

阿禾在石缝里躺到他的脚步听不见了，又躺了一会儿，才爬出来。心口那张符，已经化成了一撮灰。那个老弟子脸朝下趴在黑地边上，脖子上一圈焦黑。她把三粒黑谷包进一小块布里，塞进装禾种的那只竹筒，掏出小本子记了一笔：**冬月初一。秘境。紫须芝一株，没拔，叫人拔了。谷，三粒，黑的，不能吃。**想了想，又添了一行：**有人种过。**再往下，又是一行：**赤松观，一个。**

往前一页，是她进门前自己写的那一行：**马小宝，麻绳一盘。——凶崖？**那个人往石厅去了，嘴里念的是麻绳。她看着那个问号，看了一会儿。追上去，是一个四层撞一个九层，她死，话也带不到；喊，隔着半座秘境，谁也听不见。她把本子合上，没有往石厅走，往河床底下走——旧志上那个往外吹暖风的洞，在河床的崖腰上。一处吸，一处吹，中间是通的。凶崖底下那个人要是走投无路，往风里钻，钻出来，便是这里。

坎口上的祁长松，这时候已经走了；九层拔够了，八层也不守了。人一窝蜂涌下河床，火折子亮一个，灭一个——谁先亮，谁先死。阿禾贴着崖根摸过去，摸到那股暖风底下，在一块石头后头趴下，袖子掩着口鼻，等。她趴在那里，比石头还静。

「会自己长的土？」

小满猛一回头。他进来的那道墙缝——蛫的死身子压开的那道门——当中，不知什么时候站了一个人，赭黄袍子，白净脸，笑眯眯的，右手托着那只赤铜葫芦。他来的时候，脚底下一点声音也没有。

邹青松没急着进来。他先往四个坑沿上看了一圈，看那圈青苔，看得眼睛眯成了一条缝，像饿狗闻见了肉骨头，喉头一动，咽了一口唾沫：「[鼎苔]{注=dingtai}。筑基丹的主药，外头的丹师，一辈子见不着一根。」他这才抬眼看小满，笑意更深了，「小兄弟，你替我开的门，替我打的蛫，替我粘住了上头那六个——我跟在后头，一步路都没白走。」他伸出一根手指，冲崖上点了点，「上头那几位喊了半天娘，你听见没有？我听着，倒有点意思。」

小满想起那六个人下崖的时候，一阵一阵落下来的碎石子——里头有一阵，不是他们踩的。

邹青松往他怀里看了一眼，声音轻下去，轻得像哄孩子：「匣子放下。」顿了一顿，「人嘛——」他歪着头想了一想，像在算一笔很小很小的账，「石厅里那个胖子，你看见了。他死得快，没受罪。我这人，心软。」

小满把玉匣揣进怀里，摘下了背上的弓。这一回，他没有想藏。
story.en:
Behind the wall was a stone chamber, square, its walls of bluestone polished smooth enough to show a reflection. No herbs, no magic tools, no bones of the old ones; clean, as if swept yesterday. In the northwest corner, at floor level, was a black hole half a man high; the wind from outside the wall was being drawn into it, gust by gust. In the middle a stone altar, and on it a jade box. But the first thing Xiaoman saw as he came in was not the box. On the floor, three steps from the altar, were four pits.

Four square pits, one at each corner of a square, each the size of a bowl's mouth, a foot deep, their bottoms worn glassy, their rims worn shiny, each ringed with moss so green it was nearly black, a faint green glow under it, and close up a cool smell of bronze. His father had taught him to read hoofprints: a deep print means a heavy beast; a shiny one means it stood there a long, long time. Something very, very heavy, on four legs, had worn pits in the stone. Then it left.

Xiaoman crouched, spread his hand, set his thumb on the outer rim of one pit and spanned his way to the outer rim of the next, hand over hand — the way a hunter measures a print. One span, two, three… seven. The other three sides: seven spans each. He remembered what the old steward had told at the second test: a thousand men went down into the Si to fish up a cauldron, and didn't get it. The qi in this chamber was too thick to melt, while outside it was thin as dishwater; standing among four empty pits, he felt dimly, for the first time, that the two things might be one thing.

The four walls, up close, bore carvings, very shallow, very fine. The east wall was water, wave rolling over wave, houses floating, people floating with arms outstretched. The south wall was a man with a basket on his back, scattering something from it into the water; wherever he scattered, land rose piece by piece from under the water; his back was bent, as if under a very, very heavy load. The west wall was nine things in three rows of three, each square, on four legs, with two ears. The north wall was blank, covered in shallow squares with nothing in them; at the very bottom, against the floor, was one very small carving, cut deeper and newer than all the rest: a fox, curled up, its tail wrapped round its body — exactly like the one on the token on his chest. Yinyue jumped down from his shoulder, went to the carved fox, lowered her head and touched it with her nose, her tail hanging, then jumped back onto his shoulder without a word.

He went to the altar and opened the jade box. As the lid came up, all the qi in the room sank a little toward the box's mouth, like a roomful of water finding the low place. In it was only **a pinch of earth**. Yellow-brown, loose, just covering the bottom, no different from the soil in his family's yard where nothing grows. Xiaoman stared at it a long time. "…That's it?" But Yinyue on his shoulder said, word by word: "Breathing soil." Her voice shook; the fur on her tail tip stood up hair by hair. "Earth that grows by itself. Give it one grain, it grows a pinch; give it a pinch, it grows a mountain. Back then —" She stopped, like someone fishing in a very deep well who fished a long time and brought up only half a bucket. She stared at the four empty pits on the floor and said no more. Xiaoman waited a while, then asked: "There was wind behind that wall — did you know it was in here?" After a while she turned her head, her golden eyes bright and a little wet: "…All I could smell was something behind the wall that grows. What it is, I can't remember. I only know you're a skimmer." She turned away again, her voice low, as if talking to herself: "A skimmer, sitting on the woodpile every night till past midnight, leaking all night, sitting on. Sat a whole year. …It got on my nerves." Xiaoman wanted to say something, and what came to him was that word again, "thank you" — owed since the woodpile on Mount Meng, owed to this day and still not paid.

Her nose twitched twice more, and she sneezed. Every time she opened her mouth, the room's qi poured in. "The air in here's as strong as a jar of old wine," she said. "This king is taking a nap. Nobody disturb me." The words barely out, she became a wisp of silver light and slipped back into the token. The token went cold, cold as a stone at the bottom of a well.

He closed the jade box and sat cross-legged before the altar waiting for her to wake — the time of one meal, then another. She hadn't said what the earth was for, so he left it alone. The chamber was so quiet he could hear the wind in the black hole in the northwest corner: a draw, a pause.

Meanwhile — that day Xiaoman went down into the Cliff of Danger, and A He went with the crowd — the corridor led to the garden, and she wanted that purple-whisker lingzhi — but where the people are, more knives come down too.

Before they went in, she had seen two things: of the two map sellers, the one with his arms folded didn't push for the door with everyone else — his eyes were nailed on Shen Xiaoman; and slung across Old Wilt's shoulder was a big coil of hemp rope. You don't need that much rope to pick herbs. She made a note in her book: **Ma Xiaobao, one coil of rope. — Cliff of Danger?** and didn't look back.

She went by the map in her head. At the door of the second chamber, the third flagstone tips when you tread on it — she stood beside it and shouted, "Don't step on the third one!" One heard; one didn't hear in time, was elbowed aside by a young gentleman in brocade behind and dropped through, and an "ow!" came up out of the pit in Sun Ergou's voice. The crowd pushed her on; she looked back and shouted again; no one answered.

The stone bridge was narrow, room for one. When she reached the near end, two men had run into each other in the dark in the middle of the bridge, one of the abbey's grey robes and a green robe of the Green Duckweed school; they stopped three paces apart, neither able to see the other's face. They stood a long time, neither moving, neither giving way. The grey robe reached into his coat — and the green robe's sword was out first. The grey robe went down; what he'd been gripping was a fire-starter. The green robe stepped over him and crossed. A He crouched behind a rock at the bridgehead for a stick of incense before she dared go over.

In the herb garden past the bridge, the last plant had been pulled up by the roots. Two old disciples of the abbey pressed a young gentleman in brocade into the mud and held him there till he stopped moving, then let go and crouched in the mud to share the plant, half each; then they turned out his purse — five spirit stones, two each, and for the odd one the two of them played finger-guessing. The dry riverbed below the garden was drawn on the map as water; this year the water had sunk low and bared its bottom, and every crack was thick with spirit herbs, high, middle and low grade alike, and a vein of copper ran along the wall. Everyone poured down into it. There was only one way down, a stone step one person wide. At its lip stood the inner court's Qi Changsong, layer eight, the hem of his robe dusted earth-yellow, both feet nailed there; the crowd surged up to him, pushed him, shoved him, like water against a post — he didn't move, and it split around him and flowed back. Below the step the four layer nines were stripping the herbs clump by clump, each clump into a sleeve, not even looking at the grade. When they had enough and came up, Qi Changsong moved aside one step.

A He didn't join the scramble. She was layer four, and her art was for growing things; fighting was what she was worst at, and any of the four layer nines below, or the layer eight on the lip, could have swept her thirty feet with one sleeve. She went along the riverbed's edge toward the end where nobody was, and at the very end lay a patch of ground, black, black and shiny, not a blade of grass on it — just like her family's hillside field in Shi'ao Village. At the edge of the black ground, of all places, a plant had come up, three leaves, purple shot with gold, a fine down on their undersides glowing dark gold in the black ground like three little lamps burned nearly dry: "Purple-whisker zhi, one plant worth three spirit stones." Three spirit stones were a month's allowance in the outer court. She crouched; the black earth loosened under her fingers and showed half of something, black, hard as a pebble: grain, grain that looked burnt. She dug further down with her fingernail — under that black ground, row on row, laid out neat and even. Long, long ago, someone had farmed here. The purple-whisker zhi's roots were wound right through that row of grain: pull the plant, and roots and grain came up together in a mess of mud. She didn't pull it. From the near end of the row, well away from its roots, one grain at a time, she dug out three, and didn't hurt a single root.

As she dug out the third, something flared at the corner of her eye.

Not firelight — qi. Reading qi is the first thing the art of watching heaven's way teaches: on this black ground the qi of plants and trees rose in thin wisps of green smoke, the brightest over the purple-whisker zhi, like a lamp wick; the row of dead grain under the soil was cold, not a thread of it. But from the far side of the garden a knot of qi was coming along the riverbed's edge — on the man himself a thick layer, heavy enough to press, so that even across half the garden her chest tightened; and in his hand a ball of fire, red going on purple, stronger still than the man. Wherever that fire passed, the green smoke of the plants on either side shrank back into a single thread, as if a hand had closed on its throat.

A He's hand stopped in the earth.

The ochre robe from the riverbank with the red-bronze gourd. Layer nine, far above her; and besides, her art was for growing things and could not strike a man, and to meet him head-on was death. The fire came ten steps nearer. She looked down: a wisp of green was rising between her own fingers too — her qi, on this bare black ground, shone like a lamp.

She closed the three grains in her fist, and with her other hand felt in her sleeve and drew out a charm — of the three her master had tucked into her sleeve with the words "don't touch them unless your life is at stake," this was the first: a vanishing charm. She pressed it to her breast; a chill, and when she looked down her hands were gone, the wisp of green between her fingers was gone, even the shadow at her feet was gone. At the edge of the black ground a crack ran through the rock, a foot wide; she slid in sideways, cheek against the cool earth, and lay without moving, breathing lighter than a blade of grass.

It was him, as she'd thought: fair face, ochre robe, all smiles. He saw the three little lamps at the edge of the black ground at once. He wasn't the only one: the old disciple from the garden who had won the spare spirit stone at fists came lunging from the other side, and his hand reached the plant first. The ochre robe made no sound. His right thumb pushed, the bronze plug came out, and a fire snake shot from the gourd's mouth and went once round the man's neck. The man got out half a cry. The snake drew back; he glanced down at the gourd's mouth, and only then pushed the plug back in. In her crack A He watched it all, one thing at a time: the qi on the man himself was thick, yet to kill he spent not a thread of his own — all of it was the gourd's fire; the shield rode on his left arm, the gourd sat in his right hand; each time he struck, he pulled the plug, then put it back — and in that pull and push his eyes had to leave the man and glance at the gourd's mouth. That moment was his slowest.

He bent and pulled up the purple-whisker zhi by the roots, and the row of grain turned over into a mess of mud. Then he crouched and went through the man's coat, found three spirit stones, and tucked them away with the plant — less than three paces from her crack; she could see the mud on the sides of his boots. He stood and looked round, and his spirit sense swept low along the ground with his eyes — a chill ran down A He's spine, like a cold finger drawn across it. Her master had said that no eye below layer nine could see through this charm, and no spirit sense sweep through it. The chill slid over the crack and did not stop. The layer nines picking below the step, the layer eight guarding its lip, and this garden picked bare. Something seemed to come back to him; he smiled and said to himself, "That coil of rope at the gate…"

That coil of rope he had noticed on the riverbank: a plump young master of Chending's, and one of his hangers-on with a great coil of it slung over his shoulder. You don't need that much rope to pick herbs in the hidden realm. The Cliff of Danger got one line on the map — nobody goes. Where nobody goes is where the things are; and a coil of rope heading where nobody goes is going to tie something up. He tucked the gourd at his waist and went off toward the stone hall, fast.

A He lay in the crack till his footsteps were gone, then lay a while longer before she climbed out. The charm on her breast had already crumbled to a pinch of ash. The old disciple lay face down at the edge of the black ground, a ring of char round his neck. She wrapped the three black grains in a scrap of cloth and tucked them into the bamboo tube with the thirty seed grains, took out her notebook and wrote: **First of the eleventh month. Hidden realm. Purple-whisker zhi, one, not pulled; someone else pulled it. Grain: three, black, not edible.** Then, after a thought, one more line: **Someone farmed here.** And below that, another: **Red Pine Abbey, one.**

A page back was the line she had written herself before they went in: **Ma Xiaobao, one coil of rope. — Cliff of Danger?** That man had gone toward the stone hall with the rope on his lips. She looked at the question mark a while. Go after him, and it was a layer four running into a layer nine: she would die, and the word would never get there. Shout, and across half the hidden realm nobody would hear. She closed the notebook and did not go toward the stone hall; she went down into the riverbed — the hole the old records said blew warm wind was halfway up the riverbed's bank. One draws in, one blows out, and between them it connects. If the one under the Cliff of Danger was cornered and went into the wind, this was where he would come out.

By now Qi Changsong had left the lip of the step; the layer nines had picked their fill and the layer eight was guarding nothing. The crowd poured down into the riverbed, and fire-strikers lit and went out one after another — whoever lights up first dies first. A He felt her way along the foot of the bank to where the warm wind came down, lay flat behind a rock, sleeve over her mouth and nose, and waited. She lay there stiller than the rock.

"Earth that grows by itself?"

Xiaoman spun round. In the crack he had come in by — the door the dead guǐ's body had pushed open — there stood, who knew since when, a man: ochre robe, fair face, all smiles, the red-bronze gourd cupped in his right hand. He had come without a sound underfoot.

Zou Qingsong didn't hurry in. First he looked round the rims of the four pits, at the ring of moss, looked till his eyes narrowed to slits, like a hungry dog that smells a meat bone; his throat moved, and he swallowed. "Cauldron moss. Chief herb of the Foundation pill. Alchemists outside never see a single blade of it in their lives." Only then did he raise his eyes to Xiaoman, and his smile deepened. "Little brother, you opened the door for me, fought the guǐ for me, stuck the six up there for me — I came along behind and didn't waste a single step." He lifted one finger and pointed up the cliff. "Those gentlemen up there have been calling for their mothers half the day — did you hear? I found it rather amusing."

Xiaoman remembered the gravel that had come down in showers while the six were climbing — one of those showers hadn't come from them.

Zou Qingsong glanced at the front of his coat, and his voice went soft, soft as coaxing a child. "Put the box down." A pause. "As for you —" He tilted his head and thought, as if working out a very, very small sum. "That fat one in the stone hall — you saw him. He died fast; he didn't suffer. I'm soft-hearted, you see."

Xiaoman tucked the jade box into his coat and took the bow from his back. This time he had no thought of hiding.

exits.means: stops hiding: the bow (《落雁三箭》, the first arrow), the chase down the wind shaft to the dry riverbed — A He waiting in the dark under the warm-wind hole, two whispered lines (he kills only with the gourd; the plug's pull-and-push is his slowest moment), his arrow takes the plug, two voices from two places set four greedy men on Zou, her vine holds the shield arm one breath — and back to the ledge alone; the Hoof-It Charm from 古四, slapped on blind — its leap behind the gui; Yinyue's two hairs break the shield; he finishes Zou Qingsong himself, then, at Yinyue's word, sits in the breathing soil where the cauldron stood and lets it grow into him
exits._doors: The page's moment after this exit (story.mjs node `doors`): the five doors open one by one, a seal and a line each, in ink — colour is for 银月's memories alone.

doors.zh: 第一扇，金。「铮」的一声——是爷爷那张弓的弦。
doors.en: The first, Metal. A twang — the string of Grandpa's bow.

doors.zh: 第二扇，木。吱吱呀呀，像黑松岭的松树，在没有风的夜里自己挪了一步。
doors.en: The second, Wood. Creak by creak, like the pines of Black Pine Ridge moving a step on a windless night.

doors.zh: 第三扇，水。一冷——是那一盆洗髓的水；冷过了，化成一条清河。
doors.en: The third, Water. A chill — the marrow-washing basin; then it melts into a clear river.

doors.zh: 第四扇，火。灶膛里的火。娘拨一拨柴：「打不过就跑，跑不丢人。」
doors.en: The fourth, Fire. The fire in the stove. Ma pokes the wood: "If you can't win, run. No shame in running."

doors.zh: 第五扇，土。一股锈味儿，越开越淡——底下，是开春翻开的新土。
doors.en: The fifth, Earth. A smell of rust, fainter as it opens — and underneath, new earth turned in spring.

story.zh:
《落雁三箭》，名字是爷爷听说书听来的，爷爷一辈子没射下过大雁；他爹只教过他头一箭：先看风，后看鹿。练气二层的力气，他头一回全使在一张弓上，左臂上缠的袄襟一下子红透了，那张弓弯得比他爹拉过的哪一回都满，一箭奔面门。邹青松左臂一抬，「当」的一声，箭头撞在他左臂挎着的那面赤铜小盾上，弹了开去；盾面上的火纹，连一道白印也没有。邹青松笑道：「二层的废物，不要挣扎了。」

第二支还没搭上，邹青松左手一弹，一颗火弹先到了，小满一偏头，火弹擦着耳朵过去，燎焦了一绺头发；葫芦塞子已经拔开了，一条火蛇扑了过来。他看的不是蛇，是葫芦嘴：葫芦嘴往哪里偏，蛇便往哪里去。头一扑，他往左一滚；第二扑，往右一跳；第三扑，他跳起来，左边肋下却跟不上——蛇尾正抽在左肋上，「咯」的一声，跟十月十二那夜柴房后头一模一样。火舌舔穿了袄子，舔进皮肉，他横着飞出去，撞在石台上，眼前一白，满嘴的血腥气，左边身子像给人塞进了灶膛。他滚到西北角，那个半人高的黑洞就在手边，风一阵一阵往里吸。耳朵里是阿禾在墙根底下那一句：一处吸，一处吹，中间是通的；往风里钻，风的那头，有路。他一头钻了进去。

那是一条风道，往下斜，又陡又滑，伸手不见五指。他顺着它往下滚，怀里那只玉匣硌着断了的肋骨。不知滚了多久，身子底下忽然一空，他从一面崖壁半腰的洞口里摔了出去，在黑里落了两三丈，「噗」地落在一样软的东西上。

是个死人。

那是一道干河床——空场上卖的图，这里画的是水。他摔出来的那个洞口，在崖腰上，一阵一阵往外吹着暖风。秘境里没有天，只有石缝里几处青苔发着一点幽绿的光。他身子底下压着的，是一个本观的灰袍，早凉了，一只手攥着一把短刀，刀口缺了两个牙，另一只手攥成拳，指缝里漏出一点绿。他一口气还没喘上来，黑里伸过来一只手，捂住了他的嘴。

那只手凉，指甲缝里有土，袖口一股禾种的干香——他认得。他不动了。耳朵边上一口气吹进来，比蚊子还细，只两句：「他杀人，只使葫芦。」「拔塞子、塞塞子那一下，最慢。」那只手松开了，黑里窸窸窣窣一阵，没了。

小满趴着没动。他听得见：左边，有一个人在喘，压得极低；前头十来步，有两个，一个在磨牙；右边石头后头，还有一个。四个人，围着河床当中一丛须子又长又硬的细草——草尖上挂着一点银光，飘过来一股河底的腥凉气——都蹲在黑里，谁也不出声，谁也不先动。秘境里黑，人人都是蹲着的猎户。

头顶那个洞口里，有人落了下来，落地极轻。没有火光——邹青松把葫芦塞上了。他也是蹲黑地的人，知道谁先亮，谁先死。他的神识扫过来，河床石缝里渗着鼎气、长着灵草，扫过去处处是光，蹲着的人混在里头，分不出来；他只好拿耳朵找。

小满攥住了那把短刀，死人的指头硬了，他一根一根掰开。那人在黑里一步一步地找过来，脚步他听得见，那只葫芦他闻得见：一股硫磺味儿，在右前方，不到十步。先看风，后看鹿——黑里看不见风，看不见鹿，只剩下听。黑里射不着人。可他杀人只使葫芦——葫芦一开，就有光。小满摸出箭壶里剩下的两支，搭上一支，左手在地上摸了一块石子，往左边黑里一丢。

「嗒」。

铜塞子「啵」地一响，葫芦嘴里亮起一团红光，一条火蛇奔那一声「嗒」扑了过去，扑了个空。就这一亮，小满看见了：十步开外，一只赤铜葫芦，葫芦嘴边两根捏着塞子的指头。先看风，后看鹿——这一回，鹿自己亮了。他一箭奔那团红光去了。

「当」的一声，箭擦着葫芦嘴过去，正撞在那两根指头上，铜塞子崩飞了，滚进了黑里。火从葫芦嘴里喷了出来，一下子把邹青松照得通亮：一个人，一身黄袍，手里托着一只喷火的葫芦，站在河床正当中。塞子没了，塞不回去；他运起一身真气往葫芦口上死死一压，火压回去一半，另一半从葫芦口往外窜，像举着一支火把——他整个人便停在了拔了塞子、还没塞上的那一下，亮在那里。小满捏着嗓子，冲黑地里喊了一声，又尖又怕：「赤松观的身上有宝贝——」喊完，他已经滚开了十来步，滚过那丛草，顺手揪了一根。他这一声还没落地，另一边的黑里，隔着十几步，另一个嗓子跟着喊了，压得又粗又哑，像个饿急了的汉子：「葫芦里的宝贝，分我一点——」

黑地里蹲着的那四个，听见的是「宝贝」，一声在这头，一声在那头——要抢的不止一个，再蹲着，就没自己的份了；看见的是一个人、一团火，自己亮在那里。邹青松的眼睛往左一转，又往右一转：两个嗓子，两个地方，他那只压着火的手，不知道该往哪一头转。磨牙的那一个先扑了出去，另外三个跟着扑了上去。

那几下，小满没有看全。刀剑砍在那面盾上，「当、当、当」，火星子迸了一地，邹青松还在笑：「结丹以下——」笑声没完，他脚底下那片黑里「嗖」地窜起一根青藤，藤根拖得老长，一直拖进黑里，一圈一圈缠上了他挎盾的左臂。藤缠不住火，九层的胳膊一挣便断；可他一身的气正压在葫芦口上，要挣，得先松一头——藤便缠住了这一口气的工夫；那面盾慢了半拍。盾没有破，刀剑照旧砍不动它，可就这半拍，藤把他挎盾的胳膊往外一拽，盾沿底下露出了一截身子——他一身的气都压在葫芦口上，左臂上那层护体灵光跟着一暗，像风里的灯苗晃了一晃：一柄剑就在这一晃里钻了进去，扎进他的左膀子。邹青松一声没吭，压着葫芦口的那口气一松，火从葫芦里倒灌出来，顺着那根藤一路烧回黑里——黑里有人吸了一口凉气，极短，咬住了。跟着便是火蛇的「嘶嘶」声，一声半截的叫，又一声，跟着是一个人往黑里跑、没跑出十步便倒下的声音。四个人，没有一个喊出第二声。火光底下，邹青松的左膀子血顺着袖子往下滴，脸白得像纸；那面盾横在胸前，照旧锃亮，一道白印也没有。他拿一条火蛇往藤烧回去的那片黑里扫了一遍，扫出来的，只有一溜焦土。他没有走，蹲下去，一个一个摸那四个人的怀，摸出两块灵石、一只银镯子；又一根一根掰开风道底下那个死人的拳头，抠出一撮青苔；那丛草，连根拔了，一样一样揣好，才站起来。

小满已经在崖底下了。他把短刀咬在嘴里，抠着石缝往上爬，断着一根肋骨，左臂使不上劲，爬一尺，眼前白一下。一道缝里，指头抠着一粒圆东西，温的，一跳一跳，他攥住了，塞进怀里。爬到洞口，底下火光一转，邹青松抬起头来——射掉他塞子的那一个，怀里揣着他要的匣子，正挂在崖腰上。一条火蛇贴着崖壁追上来，舔着了他的小腿，裤腿着了火。他往底下的黑里望了一眼，什么也望不见。火追的是他，不是她。他滚进风道，把腿往土里一埋，一声没出，手脚并用，往上爬。

他从西北角那个黑洞里滚回石室，没有停，一口气冲出墙缝，冲上了石台。崖壁上那一圈青白的光还亮着，马小宝他们六个人还贴在上头。小满背贴着崖根站住了：困阵粘的是崖壁上的人——那人追出来，只要往崖上蹿一步，便下不来了。

邹青松从墙缝里出来，左膀子垂着，脸上的笑没了，只剩下一层白。他看看小满背后的崖壁，看看崖上贴着的那六个，冷笑了一声：「那阵粘什么，我在石头后头看了一炷香，比你清楚。」他把那面盾往胸前一横，抬起那只喷火的葫芦，「这一回，不跟你玩了。」

葫芦一抖，火出来，分成了四股，四条火蛇，一条从左，一条从右，一条贴着地从正面，一条绕过崖口那片黑，从他背后，一齐扑了上来。背后是崖，崖上是阵；前头是火，脚底下三四步宽，往哪边都是死。崖上有人「啊」地叫了一声。

他手往腰带里一摸，夹层里叠着一个小方块，是一张黄纸——饭桶吐出来的那匹歪马。银月嫌它丑，他也不知道它是做什么使的，只是舍不得扔。他把它往左脚底板上一拍，使足了浑身的力气，往地上一跺。

脚底板上一烫，像踩着了一块炭。他整个人离了地，离地三尺，贴着地皮横着飞了出去，四条火蛇在他身后撞成一团。他在半空里，落点由不得自己，越过了那汪小潭，「咚」的一声，一屁股坐在了一口铁黑的大锅顶上——那只死蛫，还趴在墙脚的浅窝里，脖子上插着那把剑——跟着从壳上滚了下去，滚到它背后。四条火蛇回过头来，追着他扑到，一齐撞在那口「铁锅」上，「嗤」的一声，像四瓢水泼进了灶膛，冒了一阵白烟，灭了。

是可以御火。

邹青松张着嘴，看看灭了的火，看看那只死了的蛫，看看缩在龟壳后头的小满，嗓子都劈了：「你这踏马的符是哪来的！？」

小满答不上来——他自己也是这一刻才知道。脚底那张符，已经成了一撮黄灰。

他从包袱里掏出饭桶吐出来的那只木草泥马，往地上一放。它脖子一伸，认准了主人，撒开四条木腿便追他。小满掉头就跑，绕过小潭，往邹青松的反方向没命地跑，边跑边骂：「你这个卖主的木头疙瘩！不追敌人，追我！感情你知道他是使火的是不是……」

邹青松大喝一声：「哪里跑！你以为骑上马，就快得过你爷爷我的遁术吗？看好了——」说着，他结了个火遁的印。说时迟，那时快，一息不到，人已到了三尺之内——九层的遁术，还真不是白给的。刹那间，一颗火弹已在他指尖结成。这么近，小满逃无可逃，念道：「吾命休矣。」

就在这时，木草泥马似有所感，仿佛受不住那指尖火弹的高温，只听「嘭」的一声巨响，它一下子炸成了粉末，一朵蘑菇云腾地升起，把一切都掩住了。

等那烟火散去：小满离得远些，只给掀了个跟头，滚出去两丈，爬起来，脸上黑了一层，身上倒没添新伤。邹青松就没这么好命了——那一下正炸在他指尖底下，他那面盾还挎在左臂上，来不及抬。他倒退三步，一屁股坐在地上，黄袍烧穿了半边，眉毛头发燎得精光，一张白净脸熏得乌黑，只剩两只眼睛在眨，右手五根指头焦得像五根炭条，一张嘴，吐出一口黑烟。那面盾挂在他胳膊上，照旧锃亮。

邹青松从地上爬起来，抹了一把脸，抹下一手的黑灰，又看看自己那五根炭条似的指头，眼睛红了。他把空了的葫芦往腰上一掖，咬着牙笑了一声：「好，好得很。小猎户，你这条命，我要一寸一寸地收。」

小满没等他把这口气喘匀。他攥着短刀扑了上去，脚下往左一晃——邹青松的盾跟着往左一抬，左膀子上那一剑还在淌血，盾抬得慢了半拍——小满已经拧身钻到了他右边。盾挎在左臂上，右边，是那只烧焦了的手。短刀一递，奔他右肋——

邹青松连躲也没躲。刀尖离他肋下还有半寸，那里「嗡」地亮起一层淡黄的光，薄得像一张油纸，刀尖扎上去，「哧」地滑开，只挑破了一片黄袍——护体灵光。九层的人，周身罩着这一层，一把凡铁短刀，使的是二层的力气，连他的皮也碰不着。邹青松低头看了一眼，笑了：「挠痒痒？」那只焦手攥成拳头，九层的一股气全裹在拳上，一拳捣在小满左肋上——正是断了骨头的那一处。小满整个人横着飞了出去，「啪」地摔在小潭边上，半边身子泡进了水里，嘴里一甜，一口血吐在水面上，慢慢洇开了。

他想爬，爬不起来。水冰得骨头疼——冰得他脑子一清。

邹青松一步一步走过来，抬起右手，五根焦指头捏了个诀，指尖上「噗」地冒起一点火星，跟着灭了；再捏，再冒，再灭——那只手给炸坏了，火结不成。他低头看着自己的手，那层黑灰底下，一点一点透出青来。「好，好。」他又说了一遍，掐了个火遁的印，人化作一道红影，一息便到了潭边。

小满等的就是这一下。红影落地的那一刹，他泡在水里的那只手猛地一扬，一捧潭水连泥带沙，泼在了那张脸上。火遁身上裹着的那层火「嗤」的一声，冒起一大团白汽，泥沙糊在他脸前那层灵光上，糊了个满，邹青松眼前一黑，往后一仰。小满从水里窜起来，短刀往上一撩，奔他的喉咙——

刀尖撩在他喉咙上，灵光一闪，「吱」的一声，像刮在一块石头上，滑开了。邹青松闭着眼，凭着那一声水响，盾沿横着一扫，正扫在小满拿刀的手腕上，「咔」的一声，刀险些脱了手。他抹开脸前的泥，扑了上来，盾沿顶住小满的喉咙，一路推过去，把他钉在了墙上。

墙缝那头的黑里，有人轻轻「嘘」了一声，轻得像风。

一把谷粒从黑里撒出来，撒在邹青松脚后跟底下的石缝里——石缝里还汪着小满泼出去的潭水，渗着秘境里的鼎气。谷粒落进去，「噼噼啪啪」一阵响，像锅里炒豆子，一粒一粒炸开了芽。芽一抽便是一尺，一尺便是一丈，青藤一根挨一根从石缝里钻出来，缠住了他的脚踝，缠上了他的小腿，往后一拽。

邹青松身子一晃，盾沿松了半寸。半寸就够了，小满一口气吸进来，呛得满眼是泪。

邹青松低头看了看脚底下，又抬头往墙缝那头的黑里看，笑了：「河床底下那根藤，是你吧？烧你一回，还不长记性。」他抬起那只焦手，捏诀——指尖冒一点火星，又灭了。他脸上的笑一僵。烧不了，他便拿力气挣，九层的腿一挣，藤「啪啪」地断；断一根，石缝里又钻出两根，像割不尽的韭菜。他索性撇下小满，转过身，拖着一腿的藤，一步一步往墙缝那头走：「出来。我闻见你了——一股子谷子味儿。」

小满顺着墙滑下来，坐在地上，一口一口地倒气。

墙缝里「嗖」地飞出一张黄符。符上的朱砂画的不是火，是一道一道往下坠的尖——冰锥符，高阶的，是师父那三张里的第二张。符在半空里一亮，「咔啦啦」一阵响，炸成了几十根尺把长的冰锥，白森森的，带着一股冬月河面上的寒气，劈头盖脸朝邹青松扎了过去。

邹青松把盾一横。冰锥一根接一根撞在盾上，「叮叮当当」，碎了——碎了的冰却没有落地。寒气顺着盾面往外爬，盾面上结了一层白霜，霜爬上他的左臂，爬上肩膀，往下爬到腰，爬到腿，连脚底下那一腿青藤、那汪潭水一起，「咯吱咯吱」，冻成了一坨，裹在他那层护体灵光外头，像给他套了一副冰壳子，把他整个人冻死在了石头上，只剩脖子以上露在外头。有一根冰锥钻过盾沿，扎进他左膀子上那道剑伤里，扎进去半寸，冻住了。邹青松「嘶」地抽了一口冷气。

他手上结不成火，便又掐起了火遁的印：冰壳子里头「呼」地腾起一层红光，冰一点一点地化，化成水，顺着冰壳子往下淌，「滴答，滴答」。可那冰是高阶的符冻出来的，化了一层，底下又是一层，一时半会儿化不透。他冷笑一声：「拖得住我几时？」

小满没等他把冰挣开。他从墙根底下爬起来，攥着短刀扑了上去——人冻在那里，躲不了；冰封到了脖子，他便挑没冰的地方捅。头一刀奔眼睛，刀尖扎到眼皮前头半寸，那层淡黄的灵光「嗡」地一亮，「吱」地一滑，偏了。他反手又一刀，抹脖子，刀刃贴着那层灵光刮过去，刮出一溜火星子，连一根汗毛也没碰着。第三刀扎耳根，第四刀扎嘴，刀刀都给那层光挡在外头，刀口又崩了一个牙。邹青松冻在那里，看着他捅，眼皮都没眨：「捅。捅累了，我再收你。」

冰壳子一层一层地薄下去，他脚底下淌了一地的水。

墙缝里又飞出一张符——那三张里的最后一张。符上的朱砂画的是一座山，三道横，一道竖：镇岳符。符「啪」地贴在邹青松的天灵盖上，一亮，他整个人往下一沉，像有人把一座山搁在了他肩上，脚底下的冰「咔」的一声又冻实了，膝盖弯了一弯。邹青松咬着牙，脖子上的青筋一根一根暴起来，一寸，一寸，又把腰挺直了。符上的光，一闪一闪，暗了下去。

「两张。」他喘着气笑，「观里哪个老东西，舍得给一个四层这种好东西？——还有没有？拿出来。」

没有了。

墙缝里没有声音了。小满攥着那把缺了牙的刀，站在他跟前三步远，刀尖往下滴着水。他砍过了，泼过了，跑过了，喊过了；马用了，符用了，阿禾压箱底的符也用了。他身上什么也没有了。冰一层一层地化，那张符的光，只剩下一线。他想起娘拨柴的时候说的：打不过就跑，跑不丢人——身后是崖，崖上是阵，没处跑。

他头一回这么清楚地看见了死：就在三步以外，一张熏黑了的脸，挂着一脸的冰碴子，笑眯眯的。墙缝那头，那口发抖的气，也不抖了，屏住了。

冰壳子只剩薄薄一层，透亮的，底下那层红光一跳一跳。邹青松笑了。先是嘴角咧开，跟着肩膀抖起来，最后仰起那张熏黑了的脸，笑出了声，笑得冰碴子从脸上簌簌地往下掉，笑声在崖底下撞来撞去：「哈……哈哈哈哈——一个二层，一个四层，几个稀奇古怪的手段！就凭你们——」他笑得喘不上气，眼珠子红得要滴出血来，「我在赤松观二十年，一层一层爬到九层，杀过多少人，自己都记不清了；今天叫两个娃娃烧了脸，冻了腿——好，好！先收你，再去墙缝里，把那只老鼠拎出来，当着你的面，一寸一寸地收。」

符上的光灭了。最后一层冰「哗啦」一声塌了，化成一地的水。邹青松收了笑，抖了抖腿，把那面盾往胸前一横，往前迈了一步。

胸口的木牌，便在这时烫了。

不是暖，是烫，烫得像一块从灶膛里夹出来的炭。银月从他衣襟里钻了出来，蹲在他肩膀上，薄得像一层霜。她眼皮也没抬，从自己那一条尾巴上拔下两根毛，往那面盾上轻轻一甩：「结丹？」

那面盾「咔」的一声，从当中裂开，碎成了七八瓣。两根狐毛余势不减，穿过他那层护体灵光，像穿过一张窗户纸，钉进邹青松的两条腿里，把他整个人掀了出去，撞在崖根的塌石上。他的两条腿往不该弯的地方弯着，瘫在那里，还在喘。那只赤铜葫芦滚到崖沿上，停住了。

银月蹲在他肩上，甩了甩那条拔过毛的尾巴，金色的眼睛看着他，什么也没说。

小满扶着墙站起来，咳出两口血。那把短刀还攥在手里。

邹青松瘫在塌石底下，看见他走过来，咧了咧嘴，嘴里冒着血沫子：「……我怀里有灵石。分你一半。」小满没有停。邹青松又道：「赤松观……会来要人的……」小满想起石厅拐角那个胖公子望着石厅顶的眼睛，想起河床上那四个连第二声都没喊出来的人，想起墙缝那头那口发抖的气——这个人闻见过她。这个人活着出去，石坳村、沉鼎观、他怀里的匣子、墙缝里的她，一样也藏不住。

他蹲下来。他爹放鹿血，刀从耳根底下进，一拉。他照着做了。

手是干脆的。抖是后来的事。他蹲在那里，手停不下来地抖，耳朵里嗡嗡地响。那一刀下去的手感，那一股热，淌过他的指缝，跟他十二岁那年在溪边，他爹把着他的手给那头鹿放血，一模一样。人跟鹿，原来是一样的。他扭过头去，干呕了几下，什么也没吐出来。

邹青松的袍子底下，掖着一只灰布小袋，巴掌大，袋口一道符纹——储物袋，下品的。主人死了，那道印记跟着淡了，小满的手一碰——练气的人也有一丝神识，薄得像一层窗户纸，探得开这样一只下品的袋子——袋口便开了。袋里黑沉沉的，伸手进去，比袋子深得多，像伸进一口井。里头先摸着一只钱袋，鼓鼓的，七块灵石是石厅里那个胖公子的，两块是河床上那几个人的，还有一只银镯子。钱袋底下还压着一只，更沉，袋口拿红绳扎了三道死结——这一只，是邹青松自己的。小满一道一道解开，往手心里一倒，「哗啦」一声，灵石淌了一捧，二十三块，块块青白；当中滚出一颗，比别的大了一圈，通体碧透，像一汪冻住了的泉水，里头有一缕光，自己在慢慢地转，转一圈，石室四壁便跟着亮一亮。小满两只眼睛直了。那一颗凉丝丝地贴着他的掌心，一丝一丝往掌纹里渗气，比他三个月领的灵石加在一处还冲。肩上银月「咦」了一声，尾巴尖一下竖了起来：「中品灵石。一颗，抵一百颗你那种。九层的人，攒一辈子也不见得攒得下一颗——这一颗，不知道又是从谁身上摸来的。」小满捧着那一捧，手抖起来了。他在蒙山打一冬的猎，换不来里头一块。他想起石厅里那个胖子，想起河床上那四个人。他把灵石一颗一颗数回红绳袋里，扎好，跟那只钱袋放在一处。袋里还有：河床上那丛龙须草、那撮青苔；两个小瓷瓶，一瓶回春丹，三颗，一瓶回气丹；两张黄符，画的不是火，是一道收拢的圈——敛息符，贴在身上，比你高不了几层的人，看不出你几层；一株紫须芝，根上裹着一团黑土，土里缠着几粒烧焦了似的谷。钱袋底下压着一封信，没封口，字写得歪歪扭扭：**娘：儿在观中甚好。今冬秘境，得了宝便寄钱回去，给小妹置一副嫁妆。**小满看了两遍，把信折好，跟钱袋放在一处。崖沿上那只赤铜葫芦，空着，他也捡了回来，收进袋里——赤松观的东西，挂在身上，山上便有人认得。塞子叫他射飞在河床上，出秘境那天，他从风道摸下去，摸了半天，摸了回来。地上那七八瓣赤铜盾片，铜总归是铜，他一片一片捡起来，也收了。他把储物袋系在自己腰上，道：「钱，我先替他拿着。」

「怕了？」肩上那个声音不高。小满没有答。银月道：「怕什么。这一行就是这样，你不杀他，他杀你；你今天放了他，明天死的是你，后天是你娘。刀，握稳。心，冷一点。」她顿了一顿，「可你给本王记着，你这把刀，是为什么拿起来的。忘了这个，你就是他。」她又道：「那撮土，撒在鼎站过的地方，你坐进去。你那丹田是一块沙地，雨下多少，漏多少。息壤是会自己长的土——让它长进你身子里去，长成一块厚地。厚地，存得住水。」

话音一落，她化作一缕银光，钻回了木牌。木牌冰凉，凉得像一块冰；他翻过来看，木牌背面多了一道细细的裂纹，那只蜷着的小狐狸，亮着的那一条尾巴，暗下去了一截。

邹青松腰上挂着名牌。小满解下来看背面：彭城赤松观，邹青松。他在河滩上听执事念过。他拖着他走到石台外沿，那根锈烂的铁橛子跟前，推了下去。那块名牌是铜的，他在手心里掂了两掂——铜能换钱；留着，便是一条人命挂在腰上。他把它也扔了下去。隔了很久很久，底下传上来一声。很轻，像一滴水。

潭里那个九层，他也下去翻了。腰上一只青布袋，又是一只储物袋，袋口绣着内门的云纹，印记也淡了；里头没有灵石——内门的人进秘境，不带钱——只有一瓶聚气丹，五颗，和一卷内门画的秘境图，石坎底下那一层，画得清清楚楚。他把这两样倒进自己的袋里，那只绣着云纹的空袋子，连同那人腰上的名牌，一并扔进了黑里。插在蛫脖子上那把剑，他攥着剑柄拔了两回，纹丝不动。

崖上贴着的六个人，脸朝着石头，一个声音也没有出。

他回到墙里头，把那只玉匣从怀里掏出来，打开。那撮土还在，黄褐色的，松松的，刚好铺满匣底。她说，坐进去。他把它撒在那四个空坑当中——鼎站过的地方，一圈鼎苔围着——盘腿坐了上去。

那撮土先是不动。坐了一会儿，它开始**长**。它从他身子底下往上拱，漫过脚背，漫过膝盖，漫到腰，漫到胸口，堆成一座温温的土丘，把他埋在里头，像埋下一粒种子。土里伸出一根根须子，从尾闾钻进去，往上扎进丹田，又从丹田往他身子的每一个角落里扎去，扎进经脉，扎进骨头，最后，扎进了那五扇门。那五扇门，是他的灵根，又小又乱，像一只漏勺上随手戳出来的五个洞。

须子扎进门缝，往外撑，一面撑，一面在门底下、门四周长出土来。头一扇是金，「铮」的一声，是爷爷那张弓的弦。第二扇是木，吱吱呀呀，像黑松岭的松树，在没有风的夜里自己往旁边挪了一步。第三扇是水，一冷——是那一夜泡着洗髓的大木盆；冷过了，化成一条清河，一直流到很远的地方去。第四扇是火，暖得他鼻子一酸——是灶膛里的火，他娘拿火钳拨一拨柴：「打不过就跑，跑不丢人。」第五扇是土，最沉，缝里先透出他家后院那股锈味儿，越开越淡，底下透出另一股味道来，香的，像开春头一场雨下透了，一锄头翻开的新土——吴婆婆说过：那时候，这地，是香的。

他埋在土里，浑身发抖，涨得像一片刚下过一场透雨的地，只把牙关咬得咯咯地响。他吸了一口气。石室里的灵气便动了，像一池憋了几百年的水找着了口子，全向他涌了过来。原先吸一口，漏一半，底下是沙；如今五扇门敞开着，底下长出了一块厚地，吸一口，存一口——他不是漏勺了，是一口水缸。左边那根肋骨，先是一烫，跟着一麻，再按上去，不疼了；肋下那一片烫焦的皮肉，结了痂；左小臂上那一圈牙印，也收了口。

他的手还在抖。木牌里，一个很困的声音懒懒地念了一句《尚书》{典=shangshu-hongfan}：「水曰润下，火曰炎上，木曰曲直，金曰从革，土爰稼穑。……五样脾气。土是能种东西的——种不出东西的，不叫土。你推着它们走一圈。」

他便推。一股往上拱的劲从丹田里起，拐个弯一热，热沉成暖，暖硬进骨头，又凉下来渗回丹田——木、火、土、金、水，转了一圈。他想起了他家的灶：柴烧成火，火烧成灰，灰拿去肥地，地里长出秆子，秆子晒干了，又塞回灶膛。书上一句一句写的，他娘一辈子天天在做。他的手，不抖了。

第一天夜里，二层圆满，跟着第三层的关口在他身子里「咯」地一响，像冰面上裂开一道缝。那一夜，他渴得嗓子冒烟；到后半夜，墙角石缝里「叮」的一声，渗出一道细泉来。墙后头有风，风里有潮气；有潮气，就有水。他没算错，只是算早了半夜。第二天晌午，他冲开了第四层。木牌一直是凉的。

Felling-Geese Three Arrows: his grandfather had got the name from a storyteller, and never in his life brought down a wild goose; his father had taught him only the first arrow: first read the wind, then the deer. For the first time he put all the strength of layer two into a bow — the strip of jacket on his left arm soaked red at once — and it bent fuller than any time his father had ever drawn it; the arrow flew at the face. Zou Qingsong raised his left arm — clang — the arrowhead struck the little red-bronze shield on that arm and glanced off; the flame pattern on its face hadn't so much as a white scratch. Zou Qingsong laughed. "A layer-two good-for-nothing. Stop struggling."

Before he could nock the second, Zou Qingsong's left hand flicked and a fire bolt came first; Xiaoman jerked his head aside, and it went past his ear and singed off a lock of hair; the plug was out of the gourd and a fire snake lunged at him. He watched not the snake but the gourd's mouth: wherever the mouth tipped, there the snake went. First lunge, he rolled left; second, he jumped right; third, he leapt, but his left side couldn't keep up — the tail lashed across his left ribs, crack, exactly like that night behind the woodshed on the twelfth of the tenth month. The flame licked through his jacket into the flesh; he flew sideways, struck the altar, his sight went white, his mouth full of the taste of blood, his left side as if stuffed into a firebox. He rolled to the northwest corner; the black hole half a man high was right at his hand, the wind drawing into it in gusts. In his ears was what A He had said at the foot of the wall: one draws in, one blows out, they connect; go into the wind, and at the other end there's a way. He dove headfirst into it.

It was a wind shaft, slanting down, steep and slick, pitch dark. He rolled down it, the jade box in his coat grinding against the broken rib. He didn't know how long he rolled; then suddenly there was nothing under him, and he shot out of an opening halfway up a cliff face, fell twenty or thirty feet through the dark, and landed — thump — on something soft.

It was a dead man.

It was a dry riverbed — on the maps sold on the square, this was drawn as water. The hole he had fallen from was halfway up the bank, blowing warm wind out in gusts. There was no sky in the hidden realm, only a few patches of moss in the cracks giving off a faint green glow. Under him lay one of the abbey's grey robes, long cold, one hand gripping a short knife with two notches in its edge, the other clenched, a little green showing between the fingers. Before he had his breath back, a hand came out of the dark and covered his mouth.

The hand was cool, earth under its nails, and its cuff smelled dry and sweet of seed grain — he knew it. He went still. A breath came into his ear, finer than a mosquito, two sentences only: "He kills with the gourd, nothing else." "Pulling the plug and putting it back — that's when he's slowest." The hand let go; a faint rustle in the dark, and it was gone.

Xiaoman lay still. He could hear: on the left, someone breathing, held very low; a dozen steps ahead, two, one grinding his teeth; behind a rock on the right, one more. Four people, crouched in the dark round a clump of thin grass with long stiff whiskers in the middle of the riverbed — a point of silver light on each tip, a cold river-bottom smell drifting off it — none making a sound, none moving first. It was dark in the hidden realm, and everyone was a hunter crouching.

From the opening overhead someone dropped down, landing very lightly. No firelight — Zou Qingsong had plugged his gourd. He too knew how to crouch in the dark, and knew that whoever lights up first dies first. His spirit sense swept the bed — but the cracks seeped cauldron qi and spirit herbs grew in clumps everywhere, so the sweep lit up all over, and the crouching men were lost among it; he had to search by ear.

Xiaoman took hold of the short knife; the dead man's fingers had gone stiff, and he prised them open one by one. The man came searching through the dark step by step; Xiaoman could hear the steps, and smell the gourd: a whiff of sulphur, ahead and to the right, under ten paces. First read the wind, then the deer — in the dark there was no wind to read, no deer, only hearing. In the dark you couldn't shoot a man. But he killed with the gourd and nothing else — and when the gourd opened, there was light. Xiaoman took out the two arrows left in his quiver, nocked one, felt on the ground with his left hand for a pebble, and tossed it into the dark to his left.

Tk.

The bronze plug went pop, a ball of red light woke in the gourd's mouth, and a fire snake lunged at that tk — and struck nothing. In that one flash Xiaoman saw it: ten paces off, a red-bronze gourd, and beside its mouth two fingers pinching the plug. First read the wind, then the deer — this time the deer had lit itself. He loosed straight at the red glow.

Clang — the arrow grazed the gourd's mouth and struck those two fingers square, and the bronze plug flew off and rolled away into the dark. Fire spouted from the gourd's mouth and in an instant lit Zou Qingsong up bright: one man, in an ochre robe, a fire-spouting gourd in his hand, standing in the very middle of the riverbed. The plug was gone; there was nothing to put back. He drove all the qi in his body down onto the gourd's mouth and pressed — half the fire went back in, the other half leapt out of the neck as if he held a torch — and there he stood, stuck in the moment after the plug comes out and before it goes back in, lit up for all to see. Xiaoman pinched his voice and called into the dark, shrill and frightened: "Red Pine's got treasure on him —" By the time he'd finished he had rolled a dozen paces away — over the clump, snatching one blade as he went. Before his cry had died, from the dark on the other side, a dozen-odd paces off, another voice took it up, pressed low and rough like a man half-starved: "That treasure in the gourd — give me a share —"

The four crouched in the dark heard "treasure" — one voice at this end, one at that: more than one was going for it, and whoever stayed crouched would get no share; and they saw one man, one blaze of fire, lit up there all by himself. Zou Qingsong's eyes went left, then right: two voices, two places, and the hand pressing down the fire didn't know which way to turn. The teeth-grinder sprang first, and the other three sprang after him.

Xiaoman didn't see all of what came next. Blades struck the shield — clang, clang, clang — sparks scattering over the ground, and Zou Qingsong was still laughing: "Nothing short of Core Formation —" Before the laugh was done, out of the dark at his feet a green vine whipped up, its root trailing long, all the way back into the dark, and wound itself round and round the arm that bore the shield. A vine can't bind fire, and an arm of layer nine snaps it with one wrench; but all the qi in him was pressed down on the gourd's mouth, and to wrench free he had first to let one end go — so the vine held for the space of that one breath; the shield came half a beat late. The shield didn't break, and the blades still couldn't cut it, but in that half beat the vine dragged his shield arm outward and a stretch of body showed under its rim — all his qi was pressed down on the gourd's mouth, and the protective aura on his left arm dimmed with it, wavering like a lamp flame in the wind: in that waver a sword slid in and drove into his left arm. Zou Qingsong didn't make a sound. The qi pressing the gourd's mouth let go; the fire poured back out of the gourd and ran along the vine, burning all the way back into the dark — and somewhere in the dark someone drew one sharp breath, very short, and bit it off. Then came the hiss of the fire snakes, half a scream, another, and then the sound of a man running into the dark and falling before he'd gone ten steps. Of the four, not one got out a second cry. In the firelight blood dripped down Zou Qingsong's left sleeve, and his face was white as paper; the shield across his chest still gleamed, without one white scratch. He swept a fire snake over the dark where the vine had burned back, and it turned up nothing but a strip of scorched earth. He didn't leave. He crouched and went through the four men's coats one by one, came out with two spirit stones and a silver bracelet; then, finger by finger, he prised open the fist of the dead man under the wind shaft and dug out a pinch of moss; the clump of grass he pulled up by the roots; he tucked each away, and only then stood up.

Xiaoman was already at the foot of the cliff. The short knife between his teeth, he climbed by the cracks, a rib broken, his left arm useless, his sight going white with every foot. In one crack his fingers closed on something round, warm, beating; he gripped it and stuffed it into his coat. As he reached the opening the firelight below swung round and Zou Qingsong looked up — the one who had shot off his plug, with the box he wanted in his coat, was hanging halfway up the bank. A fire snake came up the cliff after him, licked his calf, and his trouser leg caught fire. He looked down into the dark once and saw nothing. The fire was coming after him, not her. He rolled into the wind shaft, buried the leg in the dirt, made not a sound, and climbed on, hands and feet.

He tumbled out of the black hole in the northwest corner back into the chamber and didn't stop; in one breath he dashed out through the crack in the wall onto the ledge. The ring of blue-white light on the cliff still shone, and Ma Xiaobao's six were still stuck to it. Xiaoman stood with his back to the foot of the cliff: the binding held whoever was on the cliff face — if the man chasing him took one leap up the rock, he wouldn't come down again.

Zou Qingsong came out of the crack in the wall, his left arm hanging, the smile gone from his face, nothing left on it but white. He looked at the cliff behind Xiaoman, at the six stuck to it, and gave a cold laugh: "What that binding holds — I watched from behind the rocks for a stick of incense. I know it better than you." He set the shield across his chest and raised the fire-spouting gourd. "No more games this time."

The gourd shook, the fire came out and split four ways: four fire snakes, one from the left, one from the right, one low along the ground straight at him, and one curving round over the black of the drop to come at his back — all striking at once. Behind him the cliff, and on the cliff the binding; ahead the fire; under his feet three or four paces of ledge — every way was death. Up on the cliff someone cried out.

His hand went to his belt. In the hidden fold was a little folded square, a sheet of yellow paper — the crooked horse the rice-bucket had spat out. Yinyue had called it ugly, and he didn't know what it was for; he only couldn't bring himself to throw it away. He slapped it on the sole of his left foot and stamped on the ground with all the strength he had.

The sole of his foot burned as if he'd trodden on a coal. His whole body left the ground — three feet off it — and shot sideways skimming the earth, and the four fire snakes crashed into one another behind him. In midair he had no say where he'd land; he sailed over the little pool and — thud — came down seat-first on top of a great iron-black pot — the dead gui, still lying in the hollow at the foot of the wall, the sword standing in its neck — then rolled off its shell and fetched up behind it. The four fire snakes turned and came after him, and all four struck the "iron pot" at once — hiss — like four ladles of water thrown into a firebox; a puff of white smoke, and they were out.

It could ward off fire.

Zou Qingsong stood open-mouthed, looking at the dead fire, at the dead gui, at Xiaoman huddled behind the turtle shell, and his voice cracked: "Where the hell did you get that Hoof-It charm!?"

Xiaoman couldn't answer — he had only found out this very moment himself. The charm on his sole had already become a pinch of yellow ash.

He pulled out of his bundle the Grass-Mud Horse Rice Bucket had spat out, and set it on the ground. It stretched its neck, fixed on its master, and set off after him on four wooden legs. Xiaoman turned and ran, round the little pool, as hard as he could away from Zou Qingsong, cursing as he went: "You master-selling lump of wood! Not the enemy — me! You know he uses fire, don't you…"

Zou Qingsong roared: "Where d'you think you're going! Think a horse makes you faster than your grandpa's escape art? Watch this —" And he formed the seal of a fire escape. Quicker than the telling, in less than a breath he was within three feet — a layer nine's escape art is no gift. In that instant a fire bolt had already formed at his fingertip. This close, Xiaoman had nowhere left to run. "My life is over," he said.

Just then the Grass-Mud Horse seemed to sense it — as if it couldn't stand the heat of the bolt at that fingertip — and with a tremendous BANG it blew itself to powder, and a mushroom cloud rose up and hid everything.

When the smoke and fire cleared: Xiaoman, farther off, had only been bowled head over heels, rolled two zhang, and got up with a layer of soot on his face and no new wound. Zou Qingsong was not so lucky — the blast had gone off right under his fingertip, with the shield still slung on his left arm, no time to raise it. He staggered three steps and sat down hard, half his yellow robe burned through, eyebrows and hair singed clean off, his fair face smoked black so that only his two eyes blinked out of it, the five fingers of his right hand charred like five sticks of charcoal; he opened his mouth and a puff of black smoke came out. The shield hung on his arm, as bright as ever.

Zou Qingsong got up off the ground and wiped his face, and his hand came away black with soot; he looked at his five charcoal-stick fingers, and his eyes went red. He jammed the empty gourd into his belt and laughed through his teeth: "Good. Very good. Little hunter, I'll take this life of yours an inch at a time."

Xiaoman didn't wait for him to get his breath back. He went in with the short knife, a feint to the left — Zou Qingsong's shield followed it left, and with the sword wound in that arm still bleeding, the shield came up half a beat slow — and Xiaoman had already twisted round to his right side. The shield hung on the left arm; on the right was the burned hand. The knife went in, for the right ribs —

Zou Qingsong didn't even bother to dodge. Half an inch short of his ribs a pale yellow light hummed up, thin as oiled paper; the point struck it, hissed and slid off, and only slit a flap of yellow robe — a protective aura. A layer nine goes wrapped in one from head to foot, and a common iron knife with a layer two's strength behind it couldn't so much as touch his skin. Zou Qingsong glanced down and laughed. "Tickling me?" The charred hand closed into a fist with all of a layer nine's qi wrapped round it, and drove into Xiaoman's left side — right where the rib was broken. Xiaoman flew sideways and landed with a slap at the edge of the little pool, half his body in the water; his mouth went sweet, and a mouthful of blood spread slowly on the surface.

He tried to get up and couldn't. The water was cold enough to hurt his bones — cold enough to clear his head.

Zou Qingsong came over step by step, raised his right hand and pinched a sign with those five charred fingers. A spark puffed up at his fingertip and went out; he pinched again, it sparked again, went out again — the blast had wrecked the hand, and the fire wouldn't form. He looked down at it, and under the soot his face showed green bit by bit. "Good. Good," he said again, made the seal of a fire escape, became a streak of red, and in one breath was at the pool's edge.

That was the moment Xiaoman had been waiting for. As the red streak touched down, the hand he had in the water flung up a scoop of pool water, mud and sand and all, into that face. The fire wrapped round the escape art hissed into a great cloud of steam, the mud plastered the aura in front of his face, and Zou Qingsong, suddenly blind, reeled back. Xiaoman came up out of the water, the knife sweeping upward for his throat —

The point caught his throat; the aura flashed with a screech, as if the knife had scraped stone, and slid off. Eyes shut, going by the sound of the water, Zou Qingsong swept the rim of his shield sideways and caught Xiaoman's knife wrist — crack — and the knife nearly left his hand. He scraped the mud from before his face and came on, the rim of the shield against Xiaoman's throat, and drove him all the way back and pinned him to the wall.

From the dark beyond the crack in the wall someone went "shh," soft as wind.

A handful of grain came flying out of the dark and scattered into the cracks of stone under Zou Qingsong's heels — cracks still pooled with the water Xiaoman had flung, seeping with the cauldron qi of the hidden realm. The grains dropped in and went off pop-pop-pop like beans in a hot pan, bursting into shoots one by one. A shoot put out a foot, the foot became ten, and green vines came boring up out of the cracks one beside another, wound his ankles, wound up his calves, and pulled back.

Zou Qingsong swayed, and the shield's rim gave half an inch. Half an inch was enough: Xiaoman dragged in a breath and choked on it till his eyes streamed.

Zou Qingsong looked down at his feet, then up at the dark beyond the crack, and smiled. "That vine under the riverbed — that was you, wasn't it? Burned once and still haven't learned." He raised the charred hand and pinched a sign — a spark at the fingertip, then nothing. The smile froze on his face. He couldn't burn it, so he used strength: a layer nine's leg wrenched, and the vines snapped, snap, snap; for each one that broke, two more bored up out of the cracks, like chives you can never cut down. So he dropped Xiaoman, turned round, and dragging a legful of vines walked step by step toward the crack in the wall. "Come out. I can smell you — a whiff of grain."

Xiaoman slid down the wall and sat on the ground, dragging in breath after breath.

Out of the crack — whsst — flew a yellow charm. The cinnabar on it was drawn not as fire but as point after point falling downward — an ice-spike charm, high grade, the second of the three her master had given her. It flared in midair, burst with a crackle into dozens of foot-long spikes of ice, white and bristling, carrying the cold of a river in the eleventh month, and drove at Zou Qingsong from head to foot.

Zou Qingsong swung the shield across. Spike after spike struck it, ting-ting-tang, and shattered — but the shattered ice never reached the ground. The cold crept outward along the shield's face; white frost formed on it, climbed his left arm, climbed his shoulder, crept down to his waist, down to his legs, and together with the legful of vines and the pool water under his feet, creak, creak, froze into one lump, closed round the outside of his aura like a shell of ice, and froze the whole man fast to the stone, with only his neck and head left out. One spike got past the shield's rim into the sword wound in his left arm, half an inch deep, and froze there. Zou Qingsong sucked in a hissing breath.

His hand could make no fire, so he made the seal of the fire escape again: inside the ice shell a red glow rose with a whoosh, and the ice melted bit by bit, melted into water that ran down the shell, drip, drip. But that ice had been frozen by a high-grade charm: melt one layer and there was another beneath, and it would not melt through in a hurry. He gave a cold laugh. "How long do you think that holds me?"

Xiaoman didn't wait for him to get free of the ice. He got up from the foot of the wall and went in with the short knife — the man was frozen there and couldn't dodge; the ice came up to his neck, so Xiaoman picked the places the ice didn't cover. The first thrust was at the eyes: half an inch short of the eyelid the pale yellow aura hummed up, squealed, and the point slid wide. Backhand, he slashed at the throat; the edge scraped along the aura and struck a trail of sparks, and touched not one hair. The third went at the root of the ear, the fourth at the mouth; every one the light kept out, and another notch broke from the blade. Zou Qingsong stood frozen there, watching him stab, and didn't even blink. "Stab away. When you're tired, I'll take you."

The ice shell thinned layer by layer, and water spread all round his feet.

Another charm flew out of the crack — the last of the three. The cinnabar on it was drawn as a mountain, three strokes across and one down: a mountain-pressing charm. It slapped onto the crown of Zou Qingsong's head and flared, and his whole body sank as if someone had set a mountain on his shoulders; the ice at his feet cracked and froze solid again, and his knees bent. Zou Qingsong set his teeth, the veins on his neck standing out one by one, and inch by inch straightened his back again. The light on the charm flickered, and dimmed.

"Two," he said, panting and smiling. "Which old thing at the abbey would give a layer four a treasure like that? — Got any more? Out with it."

There were no more.

No sound came from the crack now. Xiaoman stood three paces in front of him, gripping the notched knife, water dripping from its point. He had cut, he had splashed, he had run, he had shouted; the horse was used, the charm was used, A He's charms from the bottom of her chest were used. He had nothing left. The ice was melting layer by layer, and the charm's light was down to a thread. He remembered what Ma said as she poked the fire: if you can't win, run; no shame in running — behind him the cliff, on the cliff the binding; nowhere to run.

For the first time he saw death so clearly: three paces off, a smoke-blackened face hung with ice slivers, smiling. Beyond the crack the shaking breath stopped shaking, and held.

The ice shell was down to one thin layer, clear as glass, the red glow beneath it leaping. Zou Qingsong laughed. First the corners of his mouth split, then his shoulders shook, and at last he threw back that smoke-blackened face and laughed aloud, laughed till the ice slivers pattered off his face, the laughter knocking back and forth under the cliff: "Ha… ha-ha-ha-ha — one layer two, one layer four, and a few freakish tricks! You lot —" He laughed till he couldn't breathe, his eyes red enough to drip blood. "Twenty years at Red Pine Abbey, climbing layer by layer to nine; how many men I've killed I can't even count — and today two children burn my face and freeze my legs. Good. Good! You first. Then I go into that crack, pull the rat out, and in front of you, take it an inch at a time."

The charm's light went out. The last layer of ice slumped with a crash into a floor of water. Zou Qingsong stopped laughing, shook out his legs, set the shield across his chest, and took a step forward.

Just then the token on his chest grew hot.

Not warm — hot, hot as a coal pulled from a firebox. Yinyue slipped out of his coat and sat on his shoulder, thin as a layer of frost. Without even lifting her eyelids she plucked two hairs from her one tail and flicked them lightly at the shield: "Core Formation?"

With a crack the shield split down the middle and broke into seven or eight pieces. The two fox hairs, their force undiminished, went through his protective aura like a sheet of window paper and drove into Zou Qingsong's legs and flung him off his feet into the fallen rock at the foot of the cliff. His legs bent where legs don't bend; he lay sprawled there, still breathing. The red-bronze gourd rolled to the edge of the drop and stopped there.

Yinyue sat on his shoulder and gave the tail she had plucked a flick; her golden eyes looked at him, and she said nothing.

Xiaoman got up by the wall and coughed up two mouthfuls of blood. The short knife was still in his hand.

Sprawled under the fallen rock, Zou Qingsong saw him coming and bared his teeth in a grin, blood frothing in his mouth: "…There are spirit stones in my coat. Half for you." Xiaoman didn't stop. "The Red Pine Abbey… will come asking for me…" Xiaoman thought of the plump gentleman's eyes round the bend of the stone hall, gazing up at the ceiling; of the four in the riverbed who hadn't got out a second cry; of the shaking breath beyond the crack — this man had smelled her. If he walked out alive, Shi'ao Village, Chending Abbey, the box in his coat, the girl in the crack — not one of them could stay hidden.

He crouched. When his father bled a deer, the knife went in under the ear, and drew across. He did the same.

His hand was clean about it. The shaking came after. He crouched there, his hands shaking and unable to stop, his ears ringing. The feel of that cut going in, that rush of heat running through his fingers — it was exactly the same as the year he was twelve, by the stream, when his father held his hand and they bled that deer. A man and a deer were the same, it turned out. He turned his head away and retched a few times, and brought nothing up.

Under Zou Qingsong's robe was tucked a small grey cloth bag, palm-sized, a rune at its mouth — a storage pouch, low grade. Its owner dead, the mark had faded with him, and at the touch of Xiaoman's hand — even at Qi Refining a man has a wisp of divine sense, thin as window paper, enough to work a low-grade pouch like this — the mouth opened. Inside it was dark and went far deeper than the bag, like reaching into a well. The first thing his hand found was a money pouch, bulging: seven stones from the plump gentleman in the stone hall, two from the men in the riverbed, and a silver bangle. Under it lay another, heavier, its mouth tied with red cord in three dead knots — this one was Zou Qingsong's own. Xiaoman worked the knots loose one by one and tipped it into his palm, and with a clatter the stones poured out, a double handful, twenty-three of them, every one a bluish white; and from the middle rolled one a size bigger than the rest, clear green right through, like a spring frozen solid, with a wisp of light inside it turning slowly by itself — and each time it turned, the four walls of the chamber brightened with it. Xiaoman's eyes went fixed. That one lay cool against his palm, seeping qi thread by thread into the lines of his hand, stronger than three months of his stones put together. On his shoulder Yinyue said "Huh," and the tip of her tail shot upright. "A middle-grade spirit stone. One is worth a hundred of your sort. A layer nine might not scrape one together in a lifetime — and who knows whose body this one came off." Xiaoman held the handful, and his hands began to shake. A whole winter's hunting on Mount Meng wouldn't buy a single one of them. He thought of the fat man in the stone hall, and the four in the riverbed. He counted the stones back into the red-cord bag one by one, tied it, and put it with the money pouch. In the bag besides: the clump of dragon-whisker grass and the pinch of moss from the riverbed; two little porcelain bottles, one of healing pills, three, one of qi-restoring pills; two yellow charms drawn not with fire but with a closing ring — qi-hiding charms: wear one and no one less than a few layers above you can tell your layer; and a purple-whisker zhi, its roots wrapped in a clod of black earth with a few charred-looking grains tangled in it. Under the money pouch lay a letter, unsealed, in a crooked hand: **Mother: your son is well at the abbey. This winter in the hidden realm, when I get treasure I will send money home, to buy little sister a dowry.** Xiaoman read it twice, folded it and laid it with the money pouch. The red-bronze gourd at the edge of the drop, empty, he picked up too and put in the bag — a Red Pine thing worn on the hip, someone on the mountain would know it. Its cork his arrow had shot off into the riverbed; on the day he left the realm he felt his way down the wind tunnel, groped a long while, and found it. The seven or eight shards of the red-bronze shield on the ground — copper is copper — he picked up one by one and put away too. He tied the storage pouch to his own waist and said: "The money — I'll hold it for him."

"Scared?" The voice on his shoulder was not loud. Xiaoman didn't answer. "Scared of what," said Yinyue. "This road is like this: you don't kill him, he kills you; let him go today and tomorrow it's you who dies, the day after your mother. Hold the knife steady. Keep your heart a little cold." She paused. "But you remember this for me: why you took up this knife. Forget that, and you are him." Then: "That pinch of earth — scatter it where the cauldron stood, and sit in it. Your dantian is sandy ground: however much rain falls, that much runs through. Breathing soil is earth that grows by itself — let it grow into you, into a thick bed of earth. Thick earth holds water."

The words barely out, she became a wisp of silver light and slipped back into the token. The token was ice-cold, cold as a lump of ice; he turned it over: on the back was a new hairline crack, and on the little curled fox, the one lit tail had gone dark along part of its length.

A name tablet hung at Zou Qingsong's waist. Xiaoman untied it and read the back: Red Pine Abbey of Pengcheng, Zou Qingsong. He had heard the steward read it out on the flats. He dragged him to the outer edge of the ledge, to the rusted iron spike, and pushed him over. The tablet was copper; he weighed it twice in his palm — copper fetches money; keep it, and he'd be wearing a man's life at his waist. He threw it after him. A long, long while later a sound came up from below. Very faint, like a drop of water.

The layer nine in the pool — he went down and searched him too. At the man's waist was a blue cloth bag, another storage pouch, the inner court's cloud pattern stitched at its mouth, its mark faded too; inside, no spirit stones — the inner court don't carry money into the realm — only a bottle of qi-gathering pills, five, and a scroll: the inner court's map of the hidden realm, the level under the stone step drawn plain. He tipped the two into his own bag; the empty pouch with its cloud pattern, along with the name tablet at the man's waist, he threw into the dark. The sword in the gui's neck he gripped by the hilt and pulled twice; it didn't budge.

Of the six stuck to the cliff, faces to the stone, not one made a sound.

He went back inside the wall, took the jade box from his coat and opened it. The pinch of earth was still there, yellow-brown, loose, just covering the bottom. She had said: sit in it. He scattered it in the middle of the four empty pits — where the cauldron had stood, ringed by cauldron moss — and sat down on it cross-legged.

At first the earth did nothing. He sat a while, and it began to **grow**. It heaved up from beneath him, over his feet, over his knees, up to his waist, up to his chest, heaping into a warm mound of earth that buried him like a seed in the ground. Out of the earth came root after root; they went in at the base of his spine, up into his dantian, and from his dantian into every corner of him, into his meridians, his bones, and last of all into the five doors. The five doors were his roots, small and crooked, like five holes poked at random in a skimmer.

The roots pushed into the cracks and prised outward, and as they prised, grew earth under the doors and all round them. The first door was Metal: a twang — the string of his grandfather's bow. The second was Wood, creak by creak, like the pines of Black Pine Ridge stepping aside on a windless night. The third was Water, a chill — the big washtub he'd soaked in the night his marrow was washed; past the chill, it melted into a clear river running far away. The fourth was Fire, so warm his nose stung — the fire in the stove, and his mother poking the wood: "If you can't win, run. No shame in running." The fifth was Earth, heaviest of all; through the crack came first the rusty smell of the yard at home, fading as it opened, and under it another smell, fragrant, like new-turned soil after the first soaking rain of spring — Granny Wu had said: back then, this land smelled sweet.

Buried in the earth he shook all over, swollen like a field after a soaking rain, grinding his teeth till they clacked. He drew a breath. The qi in the chamber stirred, like water penned for centuries finding a way out, and rushed at him all at once. Before: breathe one, leak half, with sand underneath; now the five doors stood open with a thick bed of earth grown beneath them: breathe one, keep one — he was no skimmer now, he was a water vat. The rib on his left went hot, then numb, and when he pressed it, it didn't hurt; the scorched patch of flesh under his ribs scabbed over; the ring of tooth marks on his left forearm closed too.

His hands were still shaking. From the token a very sleepy voice drawled a line from the Book of Documents: "Water soaks and descends; fire blazes and rises; wood bends and straightens; metal yields and takes new form; earth is sown and reaped. …Five tempers. Earth is what things grow in — what grows nothing isn't earth. Push them round once."

So he pushed. A force that heaved upward rose from his dantian, turned hot at a bend, sank into warmth, hardened into his bones, cooled and seeped back down — wood, fire, earth, metal, water, once round. He thought of the stove at home: wood to fire, fire to ash, ash to feed the field, stalks from the field, stalks dried and back into the stove. What the book set down line by line, his mother did every day of her life. His hands stopped shaking.

The first night, layer two was full, and then the gate of layer three went crack inside him, like ice splitting. That night his throat burned; past midnight there was a tink in the corner, and a thin spring seeped from a crack. There's wind behind the wall, and damp in the wind; where there's damp there's water. He hadn't been wrong, only half a night early. At noon of the second day he broke into layer four. The token stayed cold.
